subject: English
chapter_title: The Raven and the Fox (Fables and Folk Tales)
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 6 periods = 240 minutes
Total: 6 periods · 4h 00min

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss I (p.14): fill-in-the-blanks stanza by stanza, choosing correct option.

periods.activity_title: Reading the Fable Aloud and Unpacking Each Stanza

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud with expression, students following in their books. Pause at each stanza break to let the scene settle.
Students re-read the poem in pairs, one voice for the narrator and one for the Fox. Invite two or three pairs to share their reading with the class.

Work through 'Let us discuss I' (p.14) stanza by stanza as a whole-class activity: teacher reads each blank aloud, students call out their choice, and the class discusses why the other options do not fit.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's four rhyming couplets make it ideal for expressive read-aloud; model the Fox's flattering tone in stanza two and the triumphant 'Ha-ha!' in stanza four so students hear the tone shift. A common sticking point is the word 'morsel' — students may guess 'leaf' or 'twig'; steer them to the phrase 'would go far to seek' as a clue. The stanza-ordering task in 'Let us think and reflect I' (p.15) would make a useful independent follow-up for students who finish quickly.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss II (p.15): match seven poem words with their meanings in Column B.
Let us think and reflect II (p.16): close-reading questions on the Fox's speech and Raven's pride.

periods.activity_title: Close Reading: Fox's Flattery and the Raven's Pride

time_bands.activity: Students work individually on 'Let us discuss II' (p.15), matching the seven poem words to their meanings. Teacher circulates, then the class checks answers together with brief justifications from the poem.

Teacher reads the extract from stanza two aloud — beginning 'Sir Raven, you are a handsome bird' — and poses the close-reading questions from 'Let us think and reflect II' (p.16) to the whole class as a guided discussion.

Students write brief answers to two or three of the 'Let us think and reflect II' questions (p.16) in their notebooks. A few volunteers share; teacher consolidates why the Raven's pride made him vulnerable.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the poem aloud, students are ready to slow down and examine why the Fox's words succeed. The critical point is that the Fox addresses the Raven as 'Sir' — a form of respect — which appeals directly to the Raven's vanity; push students to explain the effect of this word choice rather than just noticing it. The personal-response question ('Imagine someone praises you too much') is rich but best saved for a quiet reflective moment; it is not anchored in class today — flag it as an interesting question to think about privately.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect I (p.15): number the four pictures in poem order.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.18): mark three statements True or False as teacher reads the crow's monologue.
Let us speak (p.18): narrate the poem as a story with a different ending.

periods.activity_title: Listening to the Crow's Journey; Retelling with a New Ending
materials: Textbook open at p.18 and p.37
Notebooks and pens for True/False marking

time_bands.activity: Teacher orients students: they will hear what happened to the crow after the fox tricked him, and must decide whether each of three statements is True or False. Students write the numbers 1–3 in their notebooks.

Teacher reads the listening transcript aloud at a measured pace (p.37 of the textbook). Students mark their True/False answers as they listen. Teacher reads the transcript a second time; students may revise. Class discusses each statement briefly, citing the words they heard.

Students prepare a brief oral retelling of the poem as a story with a different ending, using the prompt from 'Let us speak' (p.18). After a short planning pause, three or four volunteers share their versions; teacher invites the class to comment on what changed and why.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening transcript (p.37) shifts from 'raven' to 'crow' — both names refer to the same bird character in the fable; acknowledge this briefly so students are not confused when they hear 'crow' in the transcript. In the speaking activity, students often simply add 'and the raven caught the food back' — encourage richer alternatives by asking what the raven might do differently right from the start. Keep spoken turns short so several students get to share.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.18): write the fable story as a conversation, noting Raven's actions in brackets.

periods.activity_title: Turning the Story into a Dialogue Script

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the opening prompt aloud ('Reynard: Good morning, Mr Raven!…') and discusses the convention of a play script: speaker name, colon, speech, and stage directions in brackets for silent actions. Model one additional exchange on the board together with students.

Students write their own dialogue scripts independently, following the 'Let us write' task (p.18). Teacher circulates, prompting students who are stuck: 'What would the Fox say next?' and 'How does the Raven show he is pleased without speaking?'
Pairs read each other's scripts aloud in a quick rehearsal. Two or three pairs perform their scripts for the class. Class notes one thing they liked and one suggestion for each script heard.

periods.teacher_notes: The key challenge in this task is handling the Raven's silence — students often give the Raven dialogue lines, forgetting the instruction to write only actions in brackets. Remind them that the Raven holds food in his beak, so every Raven 'turn' is a bracketed stage direction. The dialogue should cover the whole arc of the poem — flattery, pride, and the fall of the morsel — so a very short script of only one or two exchanges is incomplete; guide students to include all four events.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.16): identify rhyming word pairs from each stanza of the poem.
Let us learn (p.17): pick another alliteration example from stanza two.
Let us learn (p.17): complete the opposites table and use four words in sentences.

periods.activity_title: Rhyming Pairs, Alliteration, and Antonyms in the Poem

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads stanza one aloud and highlights the pair 'limb/him'. Students work through the rhyming-pairs task (p.16) for all four stanzas in their notebooks, then the class pools answers.

Teacher explains alliteration with the example 'great big beak' from the poem, then asks students to find another example in stanza two (p.17). Students share; teacher confirms 'sweet…sing' and invites students to explain the sound effect created.

Students complete the antonyms table (p.17) individually, choosing from the word box. They then write four sentences using words from the completed table and share two sentences each with a partner. Teacher selects three or four varied sentences to discuss with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: Students at this stage often confuse rhyme with repetition — clarify that rhyming couplets end consecutive lines with the same vowel-and-consonant pattern, not the same word. For alliteration, stress that the sound, not the letter, must repeat; the pair 'such…sing' both carry the /s/ sound, which is what makes them alliterative. The sentence-writing task with antonyms is an opportunity to check whether students understand the new vocabulary in context, not merely as a matching exercise.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.19): make origami stick puppets of Raven and Fox, then enact the poem.

periods.activity_title: Puppet Theatre: Making, Enacting, and Reflecting on the Whole Fable
materials: Plain paper (A4 or similar) for origami

time_bands.activity: Students fold and assemble origami stick puppets of the Raven and the Fox using the step-by-step guide in the textbook (p.19). Teacher circulates and assists; pairs help each other.

Groups of three or four use their finished puppets to enact the poem (p.19): one student narrates while the others operate the Raven and Fox puppets. Each group performs once; the class listens for flattery, pride, and the moral.

Whole-class reflection draws the fable together: teacher asks students to name one word from the poem's vocabulary that describes the Fox, one literary device they remember, and one real-life situation where the moral — pride makes one vulnerable to flattery — might apply. Students share briefly; teacher closes by naming the fable's enduring relevance across cultures.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws on the poem's content, characters, literary devices, and moral — all of which have been explored through the chapter. Students who found the alliteration or rhyme tasks challenging may shine in the puppet enactment; the performative mode is a different strength. The reflection question about real-life situations connects the fable's moral to students' own experience, building the critical-reading habit of moving from text to world — a valued middle-stage skill.

items.item_stem: Read the lines from stanza two beginning "Sir Raven, you are a handsome bird." Which of the following best explains why Reynard addresses the Raven as "Sir"?

options.label: A
options.text: Reynard is afraid that the Raven might fly away if spoken to rudely.

options.label: B
options.text: Reynard is following the custom of greeting every bird formally.

options.label: C
options.text: Reynard respects the Raven as the oldest bird in the woods.

options.label: D
options.text: Reynard uses a polite title to appeal to the Raven's sense of importance.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Students who choose this invent a detail not present in the poem; age is never mentioned.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Suggests a misreading of the Fox's deliberate strategy as mere social convention.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Introduces a fear motivation that contradicts the Fox's confident, scheming character.

items.source_context: Raven's vanity, Fox's flattery, rhyming couplets, morsel dropped, moral in stanza four.
items.item_stem: In stanza four, Reynard laughs and says "Pride, my friend, is rather unwise." Why does the Fox call the Raven "my friend" at this moment, even though he has just tricked him? Use evidence from the poem in your answer.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Reynard calls the Raven 'my friend' with deliberate irony — it echoes the same false friendliness he used in stanza two to flatter the Raven, and now highlights how easily the Raven was deceived by a show of warmth. The Fox continues the pretence of kindness even while departing with the morsel, mocking the Raven's gullibility.

items.item_stem: Your teacher will read the following passage aloud. Listen carefully and mark each statement below as True or False.

options.text: The crow decided he was smart even without having beautiful feathers.
The crow felt cheerful immediately after losing his food to the fox.
The crow set out on a journey to share his lesson with other animals.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. False — the transcript says the crow felt really sad because the fox cheated him.
2. True — the crow says to himself 'I'm smart' even without beautiful feathers.
3. True — the transcript states he decided to go on a journey to tell all the other animals to be careful with words.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a short narrative and identifies key information to judge statements as true or false using listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Crow's sadness after being tricked, inner resolve, journey to warn other animals, moral message.
items.item_stem: After listening to the passage about what the crow did after losing his food, answer this question in one or two sentences: What lesson did the crow want to pass on to the other animals, and why did he feel the need to make a journey to do so?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The crow wanted to warn the other animals not to let pride cause them to lose what they have, which is the lesson he states as 'Do not let pride lose what you have.' He felt the need to travel and tell them in person because he had learned this the hard way and wanted to prevent others from being tricked by flattering words.

items.item_stem: Retell the story of Mr Raven and Reynard the Fox in your own words, covering all four events: Reynard's flattery, the Raven's pride, the dropping of the morsel, and the Fox's departure. Speak clearly for your classmates.

expected_elements: Mentions all four key events in the correct sequence.
Uses the characters' names: Reynard and Mr Raven.
Speaks in clear, complete sentences audible to the class.
Captures the idea that flattery caused the Raven to drop his food.

items.item_stem: Imagine the Raven sees through Reynard's flattery and does not open his beak. What do you think would happen next? Tell this new version of the story, giving a reason why the Raven's choice was wiser.

expected_elements: Presents a new ending in which the Raven keeps his morsel.
Gives a reason why resisting flattery was the wiser choice.
Uses at least one character name and stays in story register.
Expresses an opinion about pride or flattery with a supporting reason.

items.item_stem: Write the opening exchange between Reynard and Mr Raven as a short play script. Begin with Reynard greeting Mr Raven and complimenting his feathers. Remember: Mr Raven cannot speak (he holds food in his beak), so write his responses as stage directions in brackets. Include at least three turns each for Reynard and Mr Raven.

expected_elements: Uses correct play-script format: speaker name, colon, speech or direction.
Reynard's lines include flattery about the Raven's looks or feathers.
Raven's turns are bracketed stage directions, not spoken lines.
At least three turns each; the exchange builds logically toward the Raven opening his beak.

items.item_stem: Write a short diary entry by Mr Raven on the evening after he lost his morsel to Reynard. In his diary, the Raven reflects on why he was fooled and what he will do differently next time. Write at least four sentences.

expected_elements: Uses first-person voice and diary register ('Dear Diary' or similar).
Identifies flattery and pride as the reasons he was deceived.
States a specific resolve or plan for behaving differently.
Writes at least four complete, coherent sentences.

items.item_stem: The poem uses alliteration — the repetition of the same consonant sound at the beginning of nearby words. The phrase "great big beak" repeats the /b/ sound. Now write two sentences of your own, each using an alliterative pair of words. Your sentences must be about a bird or an animal.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Acceptable responses include any two sentences in which two or more words begin with the same consonant sound and the sentence is about a bird or animal — for example, 'The bright butterfly balanced on the branch' or 'The proud parrot preened its pretty feathers.' The alliterative pair must be audibly the same consonant sound, not merely the same letter.

items.item_stem: Design a simple three-panel storyboard for a puppet show of 'The Raven and the Fox'. In each panel, draw or describe the scene, name the puppet speaking or acting, and write one line of dialogue or stage direction. Your three panels must cover: (1) Reynard's flattery, (2) the Raven opening his beak, and (3) Reynard departing with the morsel and stating the moral.

expected_elements: Three panels, each clearly labelled with the correct scene.
Each panel names which puppet (Raven or Fox) is acting or speaking.
Each panel includes one dialogue line or stage direction.
Panel three captures the moral about pride being unwise.

items.item_stem: This fable was written by Jean de La Fontaine and is based on a much older story by Aesop. Research one other fable by Aesop or La Fontaine that teaches a similar moral about pride or vanity. Write a short paragraph comparing its moral with the moral of 'The Raven and the Fox', explaining which moral you find more useful in everyday life and why.

expected_elements: Names another Aesop or La Fontaine fable with a pride or vanity theme.
States the moral of the chosen fable clearly.
Compares the two morals, noting a similarity and a difference.
Gives a personal reason for preferring one moral, tied to real life.
